stem: What is this text mainly doing?
stimulus: Many athletes sit in cold water after hard workouts because they believe it speeds recovery. To test this belief, researchers had 24 runners complete an intense track session. Half of the runners then sat in 10°C water for ten minutes, and the other half rested on a bench. The next day, every runner ran a timed 200-meter sprint. The two groups' times were nearly identical, which suggests that the cold soak gave no advantage in next-day speed.
choices: Describing a study that found cold-water soaks did not make runners faster the next day
Arguing that the researchers used too few runners to support any conclusion at all
Describing a study that left unclear whether cold-water soaks affect next-day speed
Explaining how cold water changes runners' muscle tissue after a hard workout
explanation: The text sets up a belief, describes a test (cold soak or rest), and ends with a clear result: the sprint times were nearly identical. It only reports. It never criticises anything. So its job is to describe a study and give that study's actual finding. Doing this one step is what you need for the real exam question 'Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?' when the passage walks through an experiment.

B.why: You read evaluation into a text that only reports. The passage never judges the study's size or design. A 'criticize' or 'argue' choice needs the author to actually push back on something.

C.why: You stopped at 'describing a study' and didn't check the result. The last sentence gives a clear answer: the times were nearly identical and the soak gave no advantage. Saying the question was left unclear misstates the finding.

D.why: You picked an 'explain how' choice for a text that never explains a mechanism. Nothing in the passage covers what cold does to muscle. It only compares sprint times.

stem: What is this text mainly doing?
stimulus: When clover grows in a field, soil bacteria called rhizobia enter its roots and form small swellings known as nodules. Inside these nodules, the bacteria turn nitrogen gas from the air into a form that plants can absorb. In return, the clover feeds the bacteria sugars it makes through photosynthesis. When the clover later dies and decays, the nitrogen stored in its tissues is released into the soil, where the next crop planted in that field can take it up.
choices: Comparing how clover and other crops each take up nitrogen from the soil
Arguing that farmers should plant clover instead of buying chemical fertilizer
Explaining how clover, with the help of bacteria, adds usable nitrogen to soil
Explaining how clover removes nitrogen from soil, leaving less for later crops
explanation: This is a process text. Bacteria enter the roots, form nodules, and turn air nitrogen into a usable form. The clover feeds them, and when it decays the nitrogen goes into the soil for the next crop. The right choice names the whole mechanism from start to finish. On the real 'main purpose' question, a process passage almost always calls for an 'explain how' answer that covers every step, not just one of them.

A.why: This is the classic trap for process texts. The choice claims a comparison, but the text explains only one plant. 'The next crop' is mentioned only as the receiver of the nitrogen, never as something being compared.

B.why: You turned an explanation into a recommendation. The text never mentions fertilizer and never tells farmers what to do. It only describes how the process works.

D.why: You flipped the direction of the process. The text says clover adds nitrogen to the soil when it decays, so later crops get more nitrogen, not less.

stem: What is this text mainly doing?
stimulus: Folklorists long assumed that the "drowned bell" legend, in which a sunken church bell is heard ringing beneath a lake, first spread through printed collections and was only later retold aloud. To test this, folklorist Ines Marlow compared 140 dated versions of the tale. She found that spoken versions recorded by interviewers appeared, on average, eleven years before the earliest printed version from the same region. Her results indicate that the legend traveled by word of mouth first.
choices: Describing a study whose results confirm that the legend first spread through print
Describing a study whose results challenge the view that the legend began in print
Arguing that every folk legend spreads by word of mouth before it appears in print
Explaining why the legend of the sunken bell became popular in so many regions
explanation: The passage opens with an old belief (the legend began in print), describes a study that tested it, and ends with a result against that belief: spoken versions came first. So the text describes a study whose result corrects the old view. When a real 'main purpose' passage starts with 'long assumed', check whether the study supports or overturns that assumption before you pick a choice.

A.why: You matched 'describing a study' and missed which way the result went. The spoken versions came about eleven years before the printed ones. That goes against the print-first view rather than confirming it.

C.why: You stretched one legend into a rule about all legends. Marlow studied only the drowned-bell tale, so the text supports a claim about that tale and nothing more.

D.why: You answered a question the text never takes up. The study is about the order in which the legend spread, not why people liked it or how far it reached.

stem: What is this text mainly doing?
stimulus: Linguists have asked whether toddlers learn a new verb more easily when they see the action or when they only hear the word used in sentences. In one experiment, researchers taught two-year-olds made-up verbs such as "to blick." Some children watched a puppet perform each action while hearing the verb, and others heard the verb only in spoken sentences. Later, the children who had watched the actions chose the correct action for each verb far more often.
choices: Explaining how toddlers make up new verbs such as "blick" while they play
Describing an experiment that left open whether seeing actions helps with verbs
Criticizing researchers for using puppets rather than people in experiments
Describing an experiment showing toddlers learn verbs better by seeing actions
explanation: The first sentence asks a question: does seeing the action or only hearing the word work better? The experiment answers it, and the last sentence gives a clear result: children who watched the actions did far better. The text describes an experiment and gives that result. When a real 'main purpose' passage opens with a question, the right answer usually says the study answered it, so check the last sentence to confirm.

A.why: You assigned the made-up word to the wrong people. The researchers invented 'blick' to teach it. The toddlers didn't make it up, and the text is about how they learn verbs, not how they invent them.

B.why: You read the opening verb and skipped the result. The question the passage raises gets a clear answer: the children who watched chose correctly 'far more often.' Nothing was left open.

C.why: You found criticism that isn't there. The puppet is just part of how the study worked, and the author never judges it. A text that only reports can't have 'criticizing' as its purpose.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Cartographers have long debated whether people find their way more easily when a map is turned to match the direction they are facing. To test this, researchers gave sixty volunteers the same city map. Half kept north fixed at the top, and half turned the map so that the top always pointed the way they were walking. On average, the volunteers who turned their maps reached their destinations four minutes sooner and made fewer wrong turns.
choices: To explain why north has traditionally been placed at the top of most city maps
To describe a study showing that turning a map to match one's direction helped people navigate
To describe a study whose results left it unclear which way of holding a map helps people navigate
To argue that mapmakers should stop printing city maps that keep north fixed at the top
explanation: First, cover each sentence and see what it does. The text raises a question (does turning the map help?), describes how researchers tested it, and ends with a clear result: the volunteers who turned their maps arrived sooner and made fewer wrong turns. The text only reports. It never judges or recommends, so its purpose is to describe a study, and the choice must state the result correctly. B does both. This is the basic move behind every 'main purpose' question about a study or process: name the verb (describe), then check that what follows it matches the last sentence.

A.why: You took the 'long debated' opening as the topic. The text never explains why north sits at the top of maps. It mentions the debate only to set up the study, which is the real focus.

C.why: You read 'describe a study' and stopped. That is the trap in this question. The opening verb is right, but the result is wrong. The last sentence gives a clear finding (four minutes faster, fewer wrong turns), so the question was not left unresolved. Read the whole choice, not just its first words.

D.why: You turned a reported finding into a recommendation. The text says what happened in one study but never tells mapmakers what to do. 'Argue' is an evaluating verb, and this text only reports.
